entry.evidence: Thus, application of the critical taper model is often limited by an insufficient number of highly accurate profiles

steps.action: Characterized the measurement errors of the two taper inputs: slope angle from multibeam bathymetry (cited accuracy) versus basal dip from depth-converted seismic profiles (Vp range 1.7–3.4 km/s), with a simple 20 km line exercise giving up to 2.8° error in β.
steps.quote: This vertical error range is much larger than the error range of bathymetry, which is only a few dozen meters.

steps.action: Posed the problem that too few accurate depth-migrated profiles exist to resolve along-strike variation of basal friction with the critical taper model.
steps.quote: the number of accurate cross sections available for a critical taper analysis is often insufficient to reveal detailed along-strike variations

steps.action: Proposed that the effect of β on effective basal friction is small at high pore fluid pressure, so that friction can be estimated from slope angle α alone.
steps.quote: Hence, we propose that basal friction in subduction zones can be reliably estimated from only the slope angle α determined from the bathymetry.

steps.action: Reviewed the noncohesive critical taper formulas (Davis et al., Dahlen, Lehner) and illustrated them with mean wedge parameters (λ = 0.88, φ = 34°, Lallemand et al.), giving μb′ = 0.06 on the compressively critical limb.
steps.quote: Critical taper theory (Davis et al. 7; Dahlen 5; Lehner 18) is a geomechanical model based on the Mohr–Coulomb failure criterion

steps.action: Computed μb′ over a grid of α and β from 1° to 5° under mean subduction conditions and under Japan Trench outer-wedge conditions (Table 1, Fig. 3).
steps.quote: in Fig. 3B, both α and β are varied from 1° to 5°

steps.action: Compared critical state curves for β = 1° and 5° and found that at high λ the intersection lies near the curve peak, so β changes μb′ only slightly.
steps.quote: We found that β has little influence on the estimation of μb′ when the pore fluid pressure is high

steps.action: Checked the accuracy premise for α: sound-velocity-corrected multibeam depths, and a supplementary test showing that profile misalignment up to 18° from maximum slope gives under 5% error in α.
steps.quote: if the deviation from the maximum slope direction is no more than 18°, the error in α will be less than 5%

steps.action: Introduced the weight-of-alpha (WOA) parameter, A/(A+B) from a linear multiple regression of μb′ on α and β (statsmodels), obtaining WOA = 78.02% and R2 = 0.99 for the mean subduction zone.
steps.quote: we propose a parameter, which we call “weight of alpha” (WOA)

steps.action: Recomputed WOA over λ = 0–1 and φ = 20–39° (Fig. 4A), then for Japan Trench conditions (ρ = 2000 kg/m3, α and β 1–10°, Fig. 4B) and for the Kimura et al. and Wang et al. parameter sets (WOA 83.15% and 78.19%), noting low-λ exceptions such as Makran and inner Nankai.
steps.quote: we expand the parameters λ and φ to plausible ranges in nature (λ = 0–1, φ = 20–39°)

steps.action: Kept the α–μb′ approximation as a reliable proxy for the Japan Trench, with the condition that its validity be checked by a WOA diagram for each subduction zone.
steps.quote: Therefore, the variation of α could be a reliable proxy of the frictional variation along the Japan Trench.

steps.action: Chose the Japan Trench as the application case because WOA is high at the wedge toe and the 2011 Tohoku-Oki slip offers a comparison.
steps.quote: we apply this approximation to the Japan Trench, which is suitable for the application of this method

steps.action: Asked why the 2011 coseismic rupture reached the trench in this specific area.
steps.quote: we can address the question of why such a coseismic rupture occurred in this specific area

steps.action: Measured landward slope angles on bathymetric profiles within 25 km of the trench axis from the 250-m grid bathymetry of Kishimoto (2000), using GMT scripts (Table 2).
steps.quote: we used the 250-m grid bathymetry data of Kishimoto (14), focusing on the shallow portion

steps.action: Interpreted the slope angles as the relative along-strike distribution of effective basal friction at 71 points.
steps.quote: we accurately obtained the along-strike distribution of µb' on the shallow plate boundary fault at 71 points

steps.action: Compared the α distribution with the 2011 Tohoku-Oki coseismic slip from the Saito et al. (2011) tsunami inversion and found the low-α segment at about 37°–39°N inside the large-slip area (Fig. 5).
steps.quote: The low-α segment (low-μb′ segment), located at approximately 37°–39°N, corresponds to the coseismic slip distribution of the 2011 Tohoku-Oki earthquake

steps.action: Interpreted low shallow friction as letting slip propagate to the trench, and high-friction ends as barriers, making low friction a major facilitator of the tsunami.
steps.quote: the low friction in the shallow area can be considered to be a major facilitator of the huge tsunami

steps.action: Checked the low-α segment against an independent data set, the central segment defined by S-net slow-earthquake activity (Nishikawa et al. 2019), and found that the two coincide.
steps.quote: [...] low-α segment identified here approximately corresponds to the central segment along the Japan Trench (~ 37°N–39°N)

steps.action: Restricted the result to relative friction, because α variation cannot separate pore fluid pressure effects from internal friction effects.
steps.quote: it is not possible to determine whether variation in α (i.e., relative μb′) is due to a change in λ, φ, or both

steps.action: Brought in the authors' earlier full critical-taper estimates of μb′ from sparse seismic profiles (Koge et al. 2014, Fig. 5C).
steps.quote: Koge et al. (15) analyzed the Japan Trench with sparse datapoints considering non-approximated critical taper theory

steps.action: Compared the new 71-point distribution with Koge et al. (2014): high friction beyond the north and south ends of the slip agrees, but high friction near the epicenter is not found.
steps.quote: the high frictional strength near the epicenter of the 2011 earthquake documented by Koge et al. (15) was not observed in our results

steps.action: Recomputed μb′ with the full critical taper on migrated profile D6 of Park et al. (2021) near the epicenter (α = 4.69°, β = 3.26°, μb′ = 0.09), attributing the earlier high value to depth-conversion bias.
steps.quote: we obtained μb' = 0.09 in D6, with the critical taper based on the parameters of Koge et al. (15)

steps.action: Assessed global bathymetry products (ETOPO1, SRTM15+V2.0, GEBCO2021) as inputs, using cited vertical errors and a caution about merging artifacts.
steps.quote: bathymetry can be obtained from ETOPO1 (Amante and Eakins 2) or other global data sets from satellites

steps.action: Concluded that relative basal friction (slope angle) is systematically lower within the 2011 large shallow-slip area than to the south and north.
steps.quote: the seafloor slope angle (relative μb′) is systematically smaller within the area of large coseismic shallow slip during the 2011 Tohoku-Oki earthquake

No; friction is latent and is inferred from wedge geometry through critical taper theory
Estimate relative basal friction from bathymetry alone by dropping β
No rival explanations stated; the only fork is whether β matters for μb′
Not posed; no rival predictions are computed
In silico parameters set (α, β, λ, φ grids); the field case is found (Japan Trench, 2011 slip)

tree.question: 6b
tree.answer: Partly; 71 bathymetric profiles along one trench, with one earthquake for comparison
WOA stays high across λ, φ and Japan Trench parameter sets; the segment matches S-net seismicity and a D6 recomputation
Kept: α is a valid friction proxy where WOA is high; the low-friction segment matches the slip

end.claim: Where WOA is high (high pore fluid pressure ratio, low internal friction, or both), the spatial variation of bathymetric slope angle approximates the relative variation of effective basal friction, raising along-trench resolution (71 points in the Japan Trench).

decisive_move.sentence: Defining WOA from a regression of computed μb′ on α and β, which quantified α's dominance (78–83%) and made the α-only proxy checkable, is the move without which the approximation and its Japan Trench application would not exist.

gates.evidence: The β-is-small hypothesis (§2 ¶2) directed the parameter sweeps and WOA calculation, but the Japan Trench bathymetry is an existing grid (Kishimoto 2000), not acquired to test the hypothesis. The sensitivity test could have shown a large β effect, and the low-α segment could have missed the slip area. However, the slip comparison is visual, with no statistical test and no stated failure criterion (§2.3 ¶3). Nothing was declared fixed before the data were seen.

imports.item: Linear multiple regression (statsmodels API in Python) used to define WOA
Mohr–Coulomb failure criterion underlying the noncohesive critical taper model

novelty_claims.quote: The validity of the approximation can be checked with a parameter newly introduced in this study.
β has little influence on the estimation of μb′ when the pore fluid pressure is high, a consideration that had been neglected in [...]

limits: No review file was supplied, so the review sequence is not coded. Sub-claims and their statuses: (a) the relative friction distribution along the Japan Trench is estimate_with_resolution only weakly, because it is relative, has no uncertainty attached, and cannot separate λ from φ (§2.3 ¶4); (b) the correspondence of the low-α segment with the 2011 slip and the barrier interpretation is best_explanation, because no rival explanations are stated and no statistical test is made (§2.3 ¶3). The slip model (Saito et al. 2011) was chosen among debated models (Lay 2018) without reporting how other models would change the match. WOA comes from a linear regression over a bounded α–β grid, and its threshold for 'sufficiently high' is not fixed. The paper does not say when the Japan Trench comparison was decided relative to computing α (inference: probably after, since the authors' 2014 work already linked topography to the slip). The composition is coded capability_first by approximation: method development precedes the application and the question about the rupture, but no exploration phase is reported. The reference list cites Matsuzawa et al. (2015) as a cardiology meta-analysis, apparently a citation error for the VLFE study discussed in §2.3 ¶3. The text does not say what the reviewers changed.

disagreements.target: Koge et al. (2014), high frictional strength near the 2011 epicenter
disagreements.support: The 71-point α distribution shows no high friction near the epicenter, and a full critical taper on migrated profile D6 gives μb′ = 0.09; the earlier value is attributed to depth-conversion bias in the Tsuji et al. and JAMSTEC profiles.
disagreements.quote: the high frictional strength near the epicenter of the 2011 earthquake documented by Koge et al. (15) was not observed in our results

disagreements.target: Previous critical taper studies relying on β from depth-converted profiles
disagreements.support: Sensitivity calculations (Table 1, Fig. 3) and WOA show that β contributes little to μb′ at high λ, while β carries large depth-conversion errors.
disagreements.quote: a consideration that had been neglected in [...]

disagreements.target: Mean wedge parameters (bulk density 2700 kg/m3) applied to the Japan Trench toe
disagreements.support: The bulk Vp of 1.7–4.2 km/s and the Brocher Vp-density relation imply density below 2000 kg/m3, so the authors recompute WOA with 2000 kg/m3.
disagreements.quote: the assumption of a bulk density of 2700 kg/m3 for the wedge material is too high for sedimentary material

alternatives_considered.chosen: Constant pore fluid pressure ratio λ as the constraint line
alternatives_considered.alternatives: Tectonic-erosion constraint line μb′ = μ(1 − λ)
alternatives_considered.reason: In most subduction zones, fixing λ as a constant provides the constraint line; neither constraint lets friction be separated from pore pressure

alternatives_considered.chosen: Intersection with the right (compressively critical) limb
alternatives_considered.reason: The prism wedge in subduction zones should be in a constant compressively critical state just before failure

alternatives_considered.chosen: Wedge density 2000 kg/m3 and α, β ranges of 1–10° for the Japan Trench
alternatives_considered.alternatives: Mean wedge density 2700 kg/m3 and ranges of 1–5°
alternatives_considered.reason: Vp-to-density relations imply below 2000 kg/m3 near the trench; α in the Japan Trench spans 1–10°

alternatives_considered.chosen: Both Japan Trench parameter sets evaluated
alternatives_considered.alternatives: Kimura et al. (λ, φ) = (0.95, 36°) versus Wang et al. (0.8, 21.8°)
alternatives_considered.reason: Published parameter sets for the Japan Trench differ

alternatives_considered.chosen: Tsunami inversion slip model of Saito et al. (2011)
alternatives_considered.alternatives: Other coseismic slip models reviewed by Lay (2018)
alternatives_considered.reason: Most likely to be related to the deformation of the trench axis
none given for the choice; global grids are said to be sufficient because α corresponds to long wavelengths
